newsitem.title: SPAIN: Aznar says absurd to question Spain's constitution.
newsitem.headline: Aznar says absurd to question Spain's constitution.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar dismissed as absurd on Tuesday a Communist Party challenge to the country's post-dictatorship constitution.

Aznar, in comments to journalists, side-stepped a debate that has been raging since Communist Party (PCE) chief Julio Anguita said at the weekend that Spain should scrap its cherished 1978 constitution and again become a federal republic.
"He has entered the realm of the absurd," Aznar said. "The immense majority of Spaniards, and I'm among them, won't participate with the criteria that he has placed on the table."

Anguita's outburst followed two weeks of harsh attacks on the government for defying court requests to declassify secret files on a 1980s "dirty war" which the former Socialist government is alleged to have waged against Basque separatists.
The Communists contend that Aznar's conservative Popular Party (PP) government, like the Socialists before it, breached constitutional principles by refusing to hand over the documents.

But Anguita has drawn criticism from politicians of all stripes, even from members of his own United Left (IU) coalition, for suggesting that since the current constitution is being abused it should be changed.

His cry for a pre-Civil War republic was particularly contentious in a nation that holds near-fanatic reverence for King Juan Carlos, who had a key role in the return to democracy after the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.
The charismatic and thoughtful Communist leader insists that it is his democratic right to criticise the head of state and other Spanish institutions.
But his willingness to talk about PCE withdrawal from a multi-party pact defending the constitution has torpedoed chances of mounting a credible left-wing alliance in opposition to the PP government.
The PCE is the majority partner of the IU coalition, which controls 21 of parliament's 350 seats and a potential swing vote against the PP if thrown in with the Socialists.

Former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez blasted Anguita's message about the republic -- in existence before and during the 1936-39 Civil War -- and said it "seriously complicated" efforts to reach a Socialist-IU understanding.
"Looking for agreements with the political group led by Anguita is complicated when there's not even consensus on the basic elements," Gonzalez told a party congress on Tuesday.
"The Communist Party made an enormous effort to get the constitutional consensus, but Anguita's comments have put his own work in question."
